bridge: Builds on C06 processes and M01 units. Use the supplied message trace before installing packet tools.
teaching:
Start with two computers exchanging a request and reply. A protocol is an agreed set of rules for the messages: their format, meaning and permitted order. Each end of a conversation is an endpoint. A router forwards traffic toward another network; a hop is one step along the route. Instead of making one mechanism solve every problem, networks divide responsibilities into layers.

Use an addressed parcel as a limited analogy. The contents are the payload; extra information used to deliver or interpret them is a header. An application supplies the useful message. A transport protocol manages a conversation between applications. IP handles delivery across networks, and a link protocol carries a frame over the next local step. Adding a wrapper is encapsulation. The analogy explains responsibilities, but packet delivery can split, repeat or reorder pieces, unlike one intact parcel. An application message is not necessarily one packet.

A network protocol defines message meaning and exchange rules. Layering separates concerns: link delivery on a local segment, IP forwarding across networks, transport behaviour between endpoints and application meaning. A packet capture observes data at a particular location, not every event in the entire network.

An application message can span several packets, and one packet may contain only part of the message. Encapsulation adds headers around data. Addresses at different layers identify different things: a local link address is not the same as an IP address or application hostname.

Latency is elapsed time; throughput is data per unit time; loss counts data not delivered under the measurement definition. Always include units and direction. A fast link can still have high round-trip latency. If a capture begins after a connection starts, missing setup packets are a visibility limitation rather than proof that no setup occurred.

Transmission time for a packet of \(L\) bits on a link of \(R\) bits per second is \(L/R\) seconds. Convert units first: 1500 bytes is 12000 bits, so at 1 megabit/second transmission takes 12 ms. Propagation depends on path length and signal speed, not packet size. Buffering adds variable queue delay; finite queues can drop arrivals. A traceroute hop value is a round-trip measurement, with possible filtering and rate limits, not that link’s one-way delay. The video’s technology speeds and operator names describe its recording era. RFCs include different document categories; IEEE, IETF and W3C all contribute relevant standards.
example:
Application: request "hello"
Transport: TCP carries a byte stream
Network: IP forwards packets toward destination
Link: local frame reaches next hop

Teaching timing:
send at 0 ms; response at 80 ms
payload delivered: 1,000,000 bytes in 2 seconds
RTT=80 ms; throughput=500,000 bytes/s=4,000,000 bits/s
explanation: The request leaves at 0 ms and its reply is observed at 80 ms, so round-trip time, or RTT, is 80 ms. This includes the chosen request/reply measurement path; it is not automatically the one-way link delay. Throughput uses a separate observation: \(1{,}000{,}000\) bytes over 2 seconds gives \(500{,}000\) bytes per second. Multiply by 8 bits per byte to get \(4{,}000{,}000\) bits per second. A rate describes how much data arrives per unit time; a delay describes how long an event takes. The wrapper for a local link may change at a router while the application’s request continues toward the same destination.
exercise: For response times 40,60,50 ms compute mean RTT. If 2,000 bytes arrive in0.5 seconds, calculate bytes/s and bits/s. Draw which header belongs to link, IP, transport and application in a hypothetical request.
solution: Add the RTT measurements: \(40+60+50=150\) ms; divide by three to obtain mean RTT \(50\) ms. For throughput, \(2000/0.5=4000\) bytes/s, then \(4000\times8=32{,}000\) bits/s. A hypothetical packet drawing has an outer link header, then an IP header, then transport information, then application data. The exact headers depend on the selected protocols. These calculations count the stated payload bytes; they do not establish total wire traffic including headers or retransmissions.
challenge: A capture sees three packets of a five-packet transfer. Explain two reasons other than network loss that packets might be absent, and distinguish packet count from complete application messages.
challenge_solution: Capture start/end timing, capture filters and observation location can omit packets. Several packets may compose one message; retransmissions may repeat bytes. State the capture vantage point before inferring loss.
